extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and advanced law students (practitioners litigating or advising on patent licenses and remedies)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal rules governing (1) rescission, enforcement, and defenses to patent licenses; (2) recovery of license fees and royalties; and (3) interplay between contract remedies and infringement remedies in patent-license disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity will not aid licensor who has not kept his covenants
rubrics_metrics.description: That equity will not aid a licensor who has not kept his own covenants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the licensor has failed to perform his own contractual obligations, a court of equity ordinarily will not provide relief to enforce the license against the licensee. (Case citations noted.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescission of a license — mutual agreement or court action required
rubrics_metrics.description: That a license can be rescinded only by mutual agreement of the parties or by a court of equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere notice to the licensee is generally insufficient to annul a license unless the license itself provides for such a mode of rescission or equity intervenes. Cases cited: Willis v. McCollin; Brewster v. Tuthill Spring Co.; Union Mfg. Co. v. Lounsbury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of rescission when license provides for written notice
rubrics_metrics.description: That an agreement that on failure of the licensee to perform his covenants the licensor may rescind the license by a specific written notice is valid, and if the license is so rescinded further uses will have remedy either for breach of contract or for invasion of the monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the parties contractually provide for written notice to rescind, the licensor's written rescission can be effective and the parties' remedies (damages or injunction) depend on what the licensee does thereafter. See cited cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee exceeding license may be sued as infringer or for breach
rubrics_metrics.description: If the licensee uses the patented invention beyond the limits of the license or in any unauthorized way, there has been a violation of a right secured to the patentee and the licensee may be sued either under the contract or as an infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a licensee exceeds express covenants or granted scope, remedies include infringement litigation or breach of contract claims. (Goodyear v. Union India Rubber Co.; Pope Mfg. Co. v. Owsley.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages for breach measured by loss to patent rights (not double recovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the licensor adopts contract remedy the measure of damages will be the injury caused by the infringement (loss to their patent-rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The facts from which such damages can be estimated are peculiarly within the knowledge of the defendant (e.g., number/amount sold), and equity jurisdiction is appropriate to compel account/discovery to compute such damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where account/royalty information is uniquely within licensee's knowledge equity may compel discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: The ascertainment of facts to compute damages from an injury to patent-rights is peculiarly within the province of a court of equity, because the number and amount of articles sold are exclusively within the licensee's knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity may order discovery and an account to determine royalties/damages; if licensee refuses to disclose, courts may presume sales have not decreased since last account. (Cited authorities.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee sued for breach may still assert patent invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: The licensee, when sued for breach of a covenant concerning his mode of using the invention, is not estopped by the covenant from averring that the patent of the licensor is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A covenant about use does not bar the licensee from defending by asserting the patent is invalid in a contract action concerning use covenants. (Cited cases: Bliss v. Negus, Hayne v. Maltby.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee cannot justify infringement by licensor's breach of contract
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee cannot justify his infringements by the licensor's breach of contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the licensor has breached obligations, such breach does not authorize the licensee to infringe the patent; the licensee's remedy may be contractual, not to infringe. (Willis v. McCollin and others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere non-payment of royalties does not make licensee an infringer
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere non-payment of royalties does not make the licensee an infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to pay royalties typically creates a contractual claim for payment, not an immediate conversion of the licensee into an infringer, though continued breaches may have other consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocation before alleged infringement leaves former licensee with ordinary infringer defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: The revocation of a license before the alleged infringement leaves the former licensee to urge any defence open to ordinary infringers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If licensor revokes license prior to the allegedly infringing acts, the ex-licensee cannot rely on previous privileges and must defend as an ordinary infringer (subject to circumstances like whether revocation was effective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to pay license fee arises on acceptance of license (whether or not invention is used)
rubrics_metrics.description: The obligation to pay the license fee for the use of the invention arises on the acceptance of the license by the licensee; it is immaterial whether he actually practises the invention or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consideration for the license is the immunity against the prohibitions of the patent, so payments are owed until license is repudiated or rescinded. (Cited cases: McCrary, Blancbard v. Sprague.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity has jurisdiction for discovery/account where royalties involved and parties of different citizenship
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity has jurisdiction over a bill for discovery and account under a license for royalties if the parties are of different citizenship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When equitable relief (discovery, account, injunction) is necessary to ascertain royalties, equity can take jurisdiction; otherwise recovery of license fees is usually an action at law. (McKay v. Mace cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Action to recover license fees is at law unless equitable relief needed
rubrics_metrics.description: The remedy for a breach of contract to pay license fees is an action at law unless discovery or other equitable relief is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will treat straightforward fee recoveries as legal actions; equitable relief becomes appropriate when accounting/discovery/injunctions are necessary. (Ball Glove Fastening Co. v. Ball & Socket Fastener Co., McKay v. Mace.)

rubrics_metrics.name: A licensee may defend action for fees by showing failure of consideration or want of title in licensor (subject to notice/estoppel)
rubrics_metrics.description: When sued for license fees, the licensee may defend on any ground equivalent to a failure of the consideration for his contract; he may set up a want of title in his licensor unless he knew of the defect when he accepted the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the licensee accepted the license with full knowledge of adverse claims or received benefits, estoppel doctrines may bar such defenses. If he took license to quiet disputes and received the benefit, he cannot later attack title.

rubrics_metrics.name: A licensee who takes license with full knowledge of adverse claims cannot later attack licensor's patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee taking his license with full knowledge of the adverse claims against the patent, and enjoying the benefit of his license, cannot then attack the licensor's patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance with knowledge and enjoyment of benefits generally estops the licensee from subsequently denying validity; this supports stability of license arrangements. (Jones v. Burnham; Parkhurst v. Kinsman cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable jurisdiction to compel discovery/account against licensees who fail to comply with continuing obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity has jurisdiction over a bill for an injunction, discovery, and account against licensees who fail to comply with continuing obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where licensee refuses to disclose sales/production necessary to compute royalties or suppress infringements, equity may order relief (McKay v. Smith; McKay v. Mace).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumpsit or account may lie to recover for use under implied license
rubrics_metrics.description: Assumpsit will lie to recover for use under an implied license; a vendee who has an implied license to use a patented device may be liable under assumpsit for compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An implied license arising from lawful purchase gives the purchaser a right to use as long as the identity is preserved; recovery of a license fee or price may be pursued in assumpsit. (Deane v. Hodge; Hubbell v. U.S. example.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendee of a patented device cannot avoid price claim by asserting infringement without warranty/fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: The vendee of a right to use cannot enjoin the vendor from suing for the price on the ground of a prior patent unless there has been warranty or fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purchasers who buy devices that turn out to infringe other patents are generally still liable on the sales contract absent special warranties or fraud. (Cansler v. Eaton cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to pay royalties on sales arises only upon completed sale and receipt of price; any act putting article beyond licensee's control suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: The obligation to pay royalties on sales arises only when the sale is completed and the price received; every voluntary act of the licensee which places the article beyond his own control has the legal effect of a sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat transfers, shipments, or dispositions placing goods beyond control as sales for royalty purposes. Manufacture and shipment are prima facie evidence of sale. (Wilder v. Adams; Marsh v. Dodge.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty liability follows form if substance remains — equivalent elements count
rubrics_metrics.description: A royalty must be paid on devices which employ equivalent elements, as well as on those which conform to the letter of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing the form or name of an article does not avoid royalty liability if the substantial attributes employed are equivalents of the patented invention. (Wilder v. Adams.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty liability extends to articles legitimized by suits against infringers
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a licensee, in pursuance of an agreement to sue infringers, recovers damages against them and thus legitimates their sales, those sales become practically sales of the licensee and are subject to royalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the licensee sues infringers and recovers, the legitimized sales are treated as within the licensee's commerce and royalties on such sales may be owed to the licensor. (Wilder v. Adams, Adams case cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocation of license does not always terminate royalty liability for articles already made/sold
rubrics_metrics.description: Revocation of the license before alleged infringement leaves liability for royalties on articles made and sold both before and after service of notice of termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If licensor terminates a license for breach and then permits or acquiesces in certain disposals, the licensor may still be able to recover royalties for articles made and sold. (Union Mfg. Co. v. Lounsbury; cases cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Where licensee refuses to disclose books, courts may presume sales equal last account
rubrics_metrics.description: If the licensee refuses to disclose their number and amount of articles, it will be presumed that these have not decreased since the last account was rendered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to account can lead to adverse presumptions in royalty suits. (Smith v. Standard Laundry Co. cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive licensee who received full benefits cannot deny licensor's power to license or patent validity in royalty suits
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee who has received the full benefit of an exclusive license cannot, in an action thereon, deny the power of the licensor to license nor question validity of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receiving full benefit of exclusive rights typically estops the licensee from denying the licensor's authority or the patent's validity in suits for royalties or fees. (Hall Mfg. Co. v. American Railway Supply Co.; Marsh v. Dodge.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee estopped to deny validity only as to acts while license was in force
rubrics_metrics.description: The licensee is estopped to deny the validity of the patent only as to acts done while the license was in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estoppel typically covers acts during the operative license period; actions after rescission or repudiation may be treated differently. (Tibbe Mfg. Co. v. Heineker cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: A licensee knowing patent doubtful must still pay royalties while receiving benefit until interfered with
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee, knowing the patent to be of doubtful validity, is obliged to pay the royalties as long as he receives the benefit and cannot deny validity while not interfered with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts often require payment where the licensee enjoys advantages of an apparently valid patent unless eviction or invalidation occurs. (Jones v. Bamham; Marsh v. Harris Mfg. Co. cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Repudiation/right to rescind arises upon overthrow/annulment or superior title interfering with business
rubrics_metrics.description: When the patent is repealed, priority is awarded to others, or a superior title is asserted resulting in interruption of the licensee's business or new liabilities to the paramount owner, the licensee can repudiate the license and refuse to pay stipulated royalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eviction (or equivalent interruption) is the practical measure of when the licensee's liability ceases; determining what amounts to eviction in patent contexts can be complex and fact-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price for a license or sale may be unrecoverable where patent is void or device worthless
rubrics_metrics.description: That the price for a license to use the invention is not recoverable if the patent is void or the licensor has no title; where the machine is practically valueless because of infringement on a prior patent the price cannot be recovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject of the sale or license is worthless (e.g., because of prior patent), consideration may fail and buyer may have defense to price recovery. (Pacific Iron Works v. Newhall; Peck v. Farrington.)

rubrics_metrics.name: A contract to pay per item obliges to pay only for what is actually done
rubrics_metrics.description: That a contract to pay royalties per thing done obliges the licensee only to pay for what is actually done not on what might have been done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court distinctions: promises to pay per article require accounting for actual production/sales — not speculative or hypothetical amounts. (Newell v. Whitmer cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement to pay a fixed sum for first N machines is not a contract to make that number
rubrics_metrics.description: That an agreement to pay a certain sum for each of the first four hundred machines made is not a contract to make that number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obligation to make a specified number must be expressly provided; a royalty schedule alone does not create a manufacturing obligation. (Babcock v. Northern Pacific R.R. Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenant to aid in suppressing infringements binds licensee personally
rubrics_metrics.description: That a covenant to aid in suppressing infringements is binding on the licensee personally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: License covenants requiring personal action to suppress infringement are enforceable against the licensee (Washburn & Moen Mfg. Co. v. Southern Wire Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenants in license do not deprive licensee of right to show acts do not infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: That the covenants in a license cannot deprive the licensee of the right to show that his acts do not infringe the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although bound by covenants, a licensee may still defend against infringement allegations by demonstrating noninfringement of the patent. (White v. Lee cited.)
